bull_case: Warm perfusion plus NOP becomes the default U.S. workflow for complex heart/liver/lung procurement, Kidney expands the addressable organ base, and international networks replicate the U.S. model.
bear_case: Transplant volumes remain structurally limited, liver dominates revenue, alternatives such as NRP/cold perfusion improve, and reimbursement/regulatory friction caps adoption outside the U.S.
thesis: TransMedics holds genuine category leadership in a structurally changing transplant workflow. OCS replaces static preservation with portable warm perfusion and NOP integrates procurement and logistics, creating a platform rather than a single disposable. The secular runway is long, but durability is reduced by concentration in transplant medicine, liver-heavy revenue, regulatory/reimbursement dependence and operational complexity.

evidence.claim: OCS is the only FDA-approved portable multi-organ warm-perfusion platform, with heart, lung and liver approvals for DBD and DCD organs.

NOP provides end-to-end organ procurement, OCS perfusion management and dedicated air/ground logistics, allowing transplant centers to retrieve more organs without building the full infrastructure themselves.
H1 2026 U.S. OCS transplant revenue was $350.647M, led by liver $286.959M and heart $59.238M; outside-U.S. OCS transplant revenue was $10.889M.
Management is investing in OCS Kidney, Gen 3 and a European transplant-logistics network via PAD Aviation.

counterevidence: Liver accounts for most U.S. OCS transplant revenue, so organ diversification is less balanced than the multi-organ label implies.
The transplant market is regulated, reimbursement-dependent and constrained by donor availability.
NRP, cold storage/cold perfusion and competing warm-perfusion technologies remain alternatives.
Nearly all revenue is U.S.-based, limiting evidence that the model generalizes internationally.
unknowns: Five-year U.S. OCS penetration by organ.
How much transplant-volume growth is incremental versus share shift from other preservation methods.
falsifiers: If U.S. OCS transplant growth falls below transplant-market growth for several years, category leadership weakens.
If Kidney/Gen 3 fail to expand the platform, durability should be reduced.
If reimbursement rules materially reduce NOP/OCS economics, secular durability falls.

subscores.rationale: Transplant under-utilization and the shift from static preservation to active perfusion/logistics can persist for many years, with established U.S. reimbursement.
TransMedics is the only FDA-approved portable multi-organ warm-perfusion platform and has built a vertically integrated NOP distribution model.
Heart and liver are two meaningful organ markets and Kidney/international add optionality, but common reimbursement/regulatory and NOP dependencies prevent a higher diversification score.

uncertainties.rationale: Donor availability and transplant policy can constrain the addressable market even if technology adoption remains strong.
Competitive technologies can improve and NRP can substitute in some use cases.
Liver concentration and shared OCS/NOP infrastructure create correlated risk across revenue streams.
